notes: Ruling slot 0 = PPN-RDA (Diori). Slot 13 = PPN old guard/state bureaucracy around Boubou Hama. Sawaba placed in 18 (African socialism) although it has no starting popularity there: no popularity slot fits its ideology. MD sprites (MNSD, PNDS) are later organizations and not reused.

0.name: Parti Progressiste Nigérien – Rassemblement Démocratique Africain
0.english: Nigerien Progressive Party – African Democratic Rally
0.native_full: Parti Progressiste Nigérien – Rassemblement Démocratique Africain
0.text:
The Nigerien Progressive Party – African Democratic Rally is the single ruling party of Niger, led by President Hamani Diori since independence in 1960. Founded in 1946 as the territorial section of Houphouët-Boigny's RDA, it defeated its rival Sawaba in 1958–1959 and has governed alone ever since, with Boubou Hama presiding over the National Assembly.

The PPN-RDA rules through chiefs, administrators and party committees, keeping Niger firmly tied to France, the Conseil de l'Entente and Western aid. Diori, a respected mediator in African diplomacy, counts on the coming uranium revenues from Arlit and on French military protection to keep his regime secure.
0.wiki: Nigerien Progressive Party – African Democratic Rally

1.name: Les Anciens de l'UNIS
1.text:
Les Anciens de l'UNIS are the conservative notables who once formed the Union of Independent Nigeriens and Sympathisers, the pro-French party of the 1950s built around the chiefly house of Dosso. Absorbed into the ruling coalition, they keep their own identity, and Issoufou Saïdou Djermakoye remains their reference figure.

They stand for close partnership with France, respect for chiefly authority, moral order and a cautious, administrative style of government. Their base lies among Zarma aristocrats, older civil servants and the educated chiefly families of the west, and their leverage is their proven loyalty to the Western camp at the heart of the state.

2.name: Les Pontins
2.text:
Les Pontins are the graduates of the École William Ponty in Senegal, the colonial teachers' college that trained Diori himself and much of Niger's first generation of administrators, teachers and doctors. Now in their forties and fifties, they form an educated network across the ministries and schools of Niamey.

The more liberal among them want the PPN to tolerate debate, a freer press, an independent judiciary and a gradual opening to competitive elections. They favour cooperation with France and the West but chafe at personal rule and patronage. Their leverage lies in expertise and prestige: no ministry can work without them.

3.name: Union Nationale des Travailleurs du Niger
3.native_full: Union Nationale des Travailleurs du Niger
3.text:
The National Union of Nigerien Workers is the sole trade union centre of Niger, created after independence once the Sawaba-led unions had been broken. Placed under the guidance of the ruling party, it organises civil servants, teachers, transport workers and the employees of the new uranium and groundnut enterprises.

Its officials seek better wages, social insurance and the training of Nigerien cadres to replace French technicians, while avoiding open confrontation with the regime. Moderate and Western-leaning through its international contacts, the union still contains a restless rank and file, and its leverage grows with every new mine and factory.

4.name: Les Anciens de Lumumba
4.text:
Les Anciens de Lumumba are Nigerien graduates of the Patrice Lumumba Peoples' Friendship University in Moscow and other Eastern-bloc schools, many sent there through Sawaba's networks. Back home, a few work as engineers, doctors and teachers under watchful police eyes; others remain abroad.

They hold to Marxism-Leninism, call for a vanguard party, nationalisation of uranium and the groundnut trade, and a break with French tutelage in favour of alliance with the Soviet Union. Too few to act alone, they meet in private circles in Niamey and Zinder, and their leverage lies in technical skills and ties to Soviet diplomats.

5.name: Les Commandos Sawaba
5.text:
Les Commandos Sawaba are the armed militants of the banned Sawaba party who launched raids across Niger's borders in autumn 1964, followed by the grenade attack on President Diori in 1965. Trained in Ghana, Algeria and China, they were routed, many imprisoned or executed; survivors remain scattered in exile.

They believe only revolutionary violence can overthrow the PPN regime and expel French influence. Their programme mixes Sawaba's populism with guerrilla doctrine, land and trade reform and a socialist people's republic. Few in number, they keep cells among Hausa traders and migrants in northern Nigeria, and their leverage is fear: the regime still hunts them.

6.name: Hamawiyya
6.text:
The Hamallist Brotherhood follows the teaching of Sheikh Hamahullah, the Sufi master of Nioro persecuted and deported by the French, who died in exile in 1943. Present in western Niger among Zarma and Fulani communities, its adepts recite the Jawharat al-Kamal eleven times rather than twelve and keep their distance from the state.

Deeply conservative and austere, the Hamallists reject the Westernised elite, French cultural influence and the official Islam of the chiefs. Their hostility to the colonial heritage makes them receptive to any anti-Western authority, and their leverage lies in tight-knit communities, devoted followers and a long memory of martyrdom.

7.name: La Ligne dure
7.text:
La Ligne dure is the hard-line wing of the regime's security apparatus: party militants, police officers and officials who led the repression of Sawaba in the 1960s and believe Niger must be governed with a firm hand. They control the interior ministry's informers and the party's youth and women's organs.

They favour a militant single-party state on the Guinean or Algerian model, mass mobilisation and harsher controls, and grow impatient with Diori's dependence on French advisers and garrisons. Their leverage lies in surveillance, prisons and the party committees that can silence any opponent in town or village.

8.name: Communauté libanaise du Niger
8.text:
The Lebanese community of Niamey and Maradi is a small commercial diaspora, mostly Shia from southern Lebanon, active in the import trade, textiles, transport and the groundnut business. Its families arrived via Dakar and Kano and remain linked to their villages around Tyre and Nabatieh.

Its notables follow the reformist leadership of Imam Musa al-Sadr, who is building a Shia representation in Lebanon, and favour civic engagement, charity and discretion abroad. In Niger they avoid politics, cultivate ministers and lend money to traders. Their leverage lies in credit, supply networks and the goods they bring into a landlocked country.

9.name: Les Pèlerins de Karbala
9.text:
Les Pèlerins de Karbala are a handful of devout Lebanese Shia merchants in Maradi and Niamey who travel on pilgrimage to the shrine cities of Iraq and follow the senior clergy of Najaf. They gather in private prayer halls and remit religious dues to their marja'.

They hold that believers must live by religious law under clerical guidance and reject the secular habits of the younger, French-educated Lebanese. Utterly marginal in Nigerien politics, they matter only within their community, yet their transnational ties to Iraq and southern Lebanon make them a channel for the new militant ideas stirring in Shia Islam.

10.name: Tijaniyya
10.text:
The Tijaniyya Brotherhood is the dominant Sufi order of Niger, deeply rooted in the Hausa towns and increasingly drawn to the reformed branch of Sheikh Ibrahim Niasse of Kaolack. Its zawiya at Kiota, near Dosso, and its networks in Zinder and Maradi make it the backbone of established Islam.

The brotherhood preaches obedience to legitimate rulers, Sufi piety and the defence of Islamic education, and works closely with the chiefs and the ruling party. It accepts the Western partnership as long as religion is respected. Its leverage lies in the loyalty of disciples, the trading networks of its merchants and the prestige of its sheikhs.

11.name: Les Héritiers de Sokoto
11.text:
Les Héritiers de Sokoto are radical preachers and Quranic students in the Hausa border country of Maradi, Tahoua and Zinder who invoke the jihad of Usman dan Fodio and the caliphate he founded. They denounce the secular republic and the chiefs who serve it as heirs of French unbelief.

They call for a restored caliphate across the Hausa lands of Niger and Nigeria under strict Islamic law, and reject parties, elections and Western schooling. Only small bands of followers, they move freely across the open border with Nigeria, and their leverage lies in failing rains, poverty and the moral anger of rural youth.

12.name: Les Azharistes
12.text:
Les Azharistes are young Nigerien scholars trained at al-Azhar in Cairo and other Arab universities, who have returned to teach in Franco-Arab schools and mosques in Niamey, Zinder and Maradi. Excluded from the French-speaking administration, they seek a voice in public life.

They want to purify Islam of superstition, extend Arabic and religious teaching, and make Islamic morality the basis of law and education. Influenced by the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood and Arab reformism, they criticise both Sufi conservatism and Western secular values. Their leverage grows with Arab scholarships and the prestige of modern Islamic learning among the young.

13.name: Les Barons du PPN
13.text:
Les Barons du PPN are the party veterans and senior administrators who run the state machinery beside Diori: politburo members, ministers and prefects who have held office since independence. Boubou Hama, the historian-president of the National Assembly and the party's ideologue, is their most prominent figure.

They value continuity, party discipline and a cautious balance in foreign affairs, cultivating Paris while keeping doors open to other partners and to the Arab world. Their power rests on patronage, control of the groundnut and cotton marketing bodies and the administration, and on Diori's need for their loyalty in every region.

14.name: Les Chefs de canton
14.text:
Les Chefs de canton are the traditional chiefs of Niger's cantons and provinces, Zarma, Hausa, Fulani and Tuareg, who collect taxes, settle disputes and deliver the rural vote for the regime. Alongside them stand the leaders of the Tuareg confederations of the Aïr and the Azawagh.

They defend custom, Islamic order, land and grazing rights and the hierarchy of nobles and dependants, and reject both Sawaba's populism and the reformers of the capital. Non-aligned in outlook, they deal with any ruler who respects their rank. Their leverage is the countryside, where the state still governs through them.

15.name: Les Alhazai de Maradi
15.text:
Les Alhazai de Maradi are the great Hausa merchants of Maradi, Zinder and Tahoua, pilgrims to Mecca who made their fortunes as agents of the groundnut trade and in commerce with Kano across the Nigerian border. They finance the ruling party and the Muslim brotherhoods and lend to farmers.

They want free movement of goods across the border, a share of the export trade dominated by French firms and state boards, and low taxes. Cautiously loyal to Diori, they buy influence rather than seek office. Their leverage lies in credit, transport, grain stocks and the livelihoods of tens of thousands of producers.

16.name: Les Caravaniers de l'Azalaï
16.text:
Les Caravaniers de l'Azalaï are the Tuareg and Hausa traders who run the great salt caravans from Bilma and Fachi to the Hausa markets, together with the long-distance merchants of Agadez trading with Algeria and Libya. They live by moving goods across vast spaces the state barely controls.

They want freedom of trade and movement, no customs posts in the desert, no price controls and as little government as possible. Distrustful of Niamey's officials and their levies, they prefer private arrangements with chiefs and border guards. Their leverage lies in trans-Saharan routes, livestock and the supply of salt and dates to the south.

17.name: Les Pasteurs de l'Azawagh
17.text:
Les Pasteurs de l'Azawagh are the Fulani and Tuareg herding communities of the Azawagh and the northern pastoral zone, whose livelihoods depend on wells, grazing reserves and seasonal movement. The poor rains since 1968 are already shrinking pastures and killing cattle across the Sahel.

They demand protection of grazing lands against advancing groundnut farming, control of new deep wells that concentrate herds and strip the soil, and respect for nomadic life. Their concerns echo the warnings of French ecologists and FAO experts about desertification. Their leverage is the livestock economy, a pillar of exports, and the herds that feed the coastal markets.

18.name: Sawaba
18.text:
Sawaba, Hausa for freedom, is the banned socialist party of Djibo Bakary, the former head of government who campaigned for a No vote in de Gaulle's 1958 referendum and lost power to the PPN. Outlawed in 1959, it fought on from exile and launched a failed armed incursion in 1964, and Bakary remains abroad.

Sawaba stands for African socialism, the end of French tutelage, land and trade reform and power for the talakawa, the commoners, against chiefs and notables. Non-aligned with sympathies across the socialist world, it still commands quiet loyalty among Hausa traders, urban workers and youth in Zinder and Niamey.

19.name: Union des Scolaires Nigériens
19.text:
The Union of Nigerien Students groups secondary pupils and university students at home and abroad, and is the country's most outspoken critic of the regime. Its sections in Dakar, Abidjan and France are linked to the Federation of Black African Students in France and deeply marked by the events of 1968.

Its militants embrace Maoist and Third-Worldist ideas, denounce the PPN as a French puppet and demand the nationalisation of uranium, an end to the chiefs' privileges and a popular democracy independent of both Moscow and Washington. Their leverage lies in school strikes and in the future cadres of the state, who are their members.

20.name: Les Patriotes de Lété
20.text:
Les Patriotes de Lété are nationalist militants of the ruling party and its youth movement who rallied in 1963 during the dispute with Dahomey over the river island of Lété, when thousands of Dahomeyans were expelled from Niger. They keep the memory of that crisis as a test of national pride.

They call for preference for Nigeriens in jobs and commerce, the defence of every border claim and limits on foreign traders and officials. Their populism blends Zarma and Hausa grievances against the coastal elites who staff the administration. Their leverage lies in party youth sections, crowds in Niamey and the resentments of the unemployed.

21.name: La Garde du Parti
21.text:
La Garde du Parti is a militant fringe within the PPN's youth organisation and security services that dreams of a uniformed party militia on the model of authoritarian movements in Africa and Europe. Its members admire discipline, parades and the cult of the leader.

They advocate a totally mobilised nation, compulsory civic service, the eradication of Sawaba and of every ethnic or religious faction, and a single will imposed from Niamey. Lacking a leader of stature, they remain a pressure group, but their leverage lies in the armed party volunteers who helped hunt down Sawaba commandos in 1964.

22.name: Forces Armées Nigériennes
22.text:
The Niger Armed Forces are a small army of a few battalions formed at independence from former colonial troops, supported by French officers and a French garrison in Niamey. Diori keeps them under close watch and relies more on his gendarmerie and French guarantees, but the officer corps, including Seyni Kountché, is growing in confidence.

The officers see themselves as guardians of national unity and are dismayed by corruption and the regime's patronage. Loyal to the Western alliance, they watch the coups in Dahomey, Togo and Mali closely. Their leverage is the monopoly of force in a state with few strong institutions.

23.name: Sultanat du Damagaram
23.text:
The Sultanate of Damagaram is the Kanuri and Hausa monarchy of Zinder, which dominated the trans-Saharan trade of the east before the French conquest of 1899. Its sultan still presides over a court, councillors and district heads, and remains one of the most prestigious traditional rulers in Niger.

The sultanate seeks the preservation of royal authority, Islamic custom and court ceremony, and a role in local justice and administration. It works with the ruling party but remembers Zinder's former primacy over Niamey. Its leverage lies in the loyalty of the eastern Hausa and Kanuri and in its ties with the emirates of northern Nigeria.
